## Pine Labs P3P (Company Product)

P3P (Pine Labs Payments Protocol) is an enterprise offering at Pine Labs for agentic payments. It implements an HTTP-native x402 payment flow over UPI ReservePay / SBMD so AI agents and applications can pay for resources with human-approved budgets.

Goutham’s role: SDK handling and making the SDKs enterprise-ready.

Ownership themes:

- TypeScript and Python client/server SDK surfaces.
- 402 challenge → token → Payment credential → capture → Payment-Receipt flow.
- Auth modes, concurrent refresh, payment-method selection, pending-debit semantics.
- Grantex integration for delegated agent spend controls.
- Multi-language parity and public packaging.

Public links:

- https://www.npmjs.com/package/p3p-client-sdk
- https://www.npmjs.com/package/p3p-server-sdk
- https://pypi.org/project/pinelabs-online-p3p-client-sdk/
- https://pypi.org/project/pinelabs-online-p3p-server-sdk/
- https://grantex.dev

This section is higher priority than MCP Nexus because it is company product work, not a personal side project.

## MCP Nexus (Personal Side Project)

MCP Nexus is a personal AI-assisted research prototype for a secure gateway over multiple registered provider MCPs. It is not a Pine Labs product and not a production SaaS claim.

Problem:

AI clients can connect to many MCP servers, but direct one-off integrations make provider discovery, tool permissions, tokens, and auditability fragmented.

Approach:

Prototype a gateway that registers provider MCPs, routes approved tool calls, and adds governance controls such as validation, permissions, audit logs, rate limits, and confirmations.

## Goose (Personal Open Source)

Goose is a lightweight, cloud-native Kafka-to-sink firehose built in Go — a 25x lighter replacement for raystack firehose (786MB Java → 33MB Go binary). It is a personal open-source project in the Goose-Kafka GitHub org, not a Pine Labs product.

Problem:

Raystack firehose is the standard Kafka-to-HTTP firehose at scale, but it ships as a 786MB Java application with 50+ dependencies, ~300MB RAM at idle, and a connection pinning bug that causes uneven load distribution across backend pods.

Approach:

Rebuilt the firehose in Go with a worker-pool architecture, channel-based backpressure, contiguity-gated offset commits, batch-poll consumer with chunk splitting, and a pluggable sink interface supporting 5 sink types. Production-hardened with Cosign image signing, SBOM, Trivy scanning, NetworkPolicy, and PDB.

Key metrics:

- 33MB Go binary (25x smaller than Java firehose)
- 13–23 MiB RAM at load (vs ~300MB Java)
- 6,017 msg/s at 0ms sink delay, ~4,000 msg/s at 50ms delay
- Zero message drops (network error retry fix)
- <1s startup (vs 5–10s JVM)

Features:

- 5 sink types: HTTP, gRPC, MongoDB, PostgreSQL, Redis
- CEL filtering + schema validation
- Protobuf→JSON conversion via Stencil schema registry
- Circuit breaker with sliding window
- Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) with metadata headers
- Batch-poll consumer with chunk splitting (ordered vs multi-worker modes)
- 15 Prometheus metrics + OpenTelemetry traces
- Helm chart with HPA, NetworkPolicy, PDB, security context
- TDD: 82 unit tests (-race), 18 integration tests

Public links:

- https://github.com/Goose-Kafka/goose — source code, v1.1.0 released
- https://goose-kafka.mintlify.site/ — documentation (35+ pages)
- https://goose-kafka.github.io/goose/ — marketing website
- https://github.com/Goose-Kafka/goose-integration-test — integration tests

Ownership: Entire project end-to-end — architecture, implementation, CI/CD, Docker/Helm, integration tests, load testing, documentation, release management. Used AI-assisted development (Copilot CLI) as the implementer while directing all architectural decisions.
